Tissues from cancer patients often include tumor areas alongside healthy regions, which are visually captured through various digitized section methods. In these images, sections of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs)—immune cells found among tumor boundaries—serve as critical indicators of a patient's condition. Since identifying TILs requires specialized knowledge, their manual counting and placement are time-intensive. This study outlines a machine learning strategy to predict TIL locations within images by utilizing a dataset of 1,000 square sections (each 100x100 pixels) of tissue. The model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) score of 0.875 during testing. By comparing predicted TIL positions against "expert-annotated" TIL locations in the training image set, the authors found an 85% agreement rate, signifying strong performance. TIL location predictions were further evaluated by non-specialist pathologists, a process that outperformed prior methods published in 2017. This approach offers a robust tool for analyzing TIL distribution in digitized tissue images.

Two-dimensional magnetic materials are highly valuable in cavity magnomechanics, a subfield that utilizes magnetic materials to facilitate robust quantum-state engineering. To improve upon existing systems, which often rely on cumbersome arrangements to achieve strong magnon-photon coupling, we introduce a 2D material, FeP$_3$, as a thin, flat coating on a dielectric cavity qutrit. We analyze the intrinsic material properties and demonstrate that a single layer of FeP$_3$ can effectively double the cavity qutrit's resonant frequency splitting. Additionally, we examine magnon-photon interactions, confirming that strong coupling can be maintained even with just a monolayer. These findings suggest that replacing volume-based ferromagnets in future magnon-photon systems with thin, two-dimensional materials will be a promising development.

By allowing the policy to independently adjust a gait selection input from the array of available skills, the learned policy outperforms methods that rely solely on a single fixed rhythm, demonstrating better structural resilience and fewer dropped items during falls. Future work will aim to generalize results across a variety of real-world objects and environments.

The Graphical Lasso method provides a way to estimate conditional independence structures among variables with sparse precision matrices, which may arise from multivariate Gaussian distributions or specific non-Gaussian models. I present a new, more general framework for this modeling that includes "Latent-Graphical Lasso," which accounts for unobserved latent variables by partitioning the precision matrix into sub-blocks. By treating each sub-block corresponding to a latent variable as a random draw from a scaled inverse-Wishart distribution with specific hyperparameters, we can perform efficient sampling via Gibbs Markov Chain Monte Carlo. This approach supports both sparse and dense estimation of the sub-blocks, facilitating robust inference of the latent variables. Additionally, I will discuss how these algorithms, including a variant estimated for high-dimensional settings, can be applied for clustering and identifying latent groups.

Traditional auto-correlation methods for pitch detection are often compromised by background noise, resulting in inaccurate pitch estimates. To address this, a novel algorithm called RaRCP (Real-time Analysis of Short-term Auto-correlation with Peak selection) is introduced. This system includes an auto-correlation-based module for primary pitch value estimation, a peak selection sub-module designed to refine these values, and a high-speed, low-latency auto-focusing mechanism. The core goal of RaRCP is to produce accurate pitch and fundamental frequency ($f_0$) readings in real-time, regardless of acoustic environments. The system operates with a processing latency of under 10ms and operates on 10Hz input samples. The inclusion of a user-adjustable parameter allows the system to balance accuracy against computation time based on specific application needs. The study also outlines the mathematical models governing auto-peak identification and a strategy for auto-focusing, demonstrating the system's effectiveness through comprehensive experimental analysis.

In this paper, we investigate and prove the robustness of the derivative-free and over-relaxed infinite-dimensional Anderson acceleration (DWIFOB) for homotopy coupling schemes applied to variational inequalities. This method does not require the Jacobian matrices of a certain class of variational inequality problems, nor the smoothing derivations. Our results demonstrate that, regarding its robustness, DWIFOB outperforms the standard regularized Anderson acceleration. Additionally, we establish a sufficient condition, in the form of an $\Omega$-test function. This condition ensures superlinear convergence and generalizes the sufficient condition previously identified by OLSON and others for problems that are smooth and differentiable.

This research presents a low-complexity method for joint multiple antenna selection and mmWave multicasting resource allocation. By leveraging the benefits of receiving multiple antennas—a capability not frequently explored in existing literature—our approach achieves beamforming performance gains without significantly increasing computational demands. Specifically, the problem of selecting the optimal receiving antenna set from an array is framed as a binary search, allowing for selection of the precise strong channels identified in prior high-complexity solutions. Consequently, our technique delivers similar throughput performance while reducing computational complexity by three orders of magnitude, as as verified through simulations.

This work addresses user influence prediction within social networks, a critical task with broad implications. Motion planning in dynamic settings presents a well-known difficulty that deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods have attempted to address. However, these recent deep RL approaches are not truly motion planning methods; they are robot control strategies. True motion planning, not raw robot control, represents the action selection process. In this work, we reframe deep RL as a meta-learning problem where the goal is to learn a policy for selecting actions. Our proposed Heterogeneous Policy Learning (HPL) framework utilizes a policy network to select a specific surrogate policy from a predefined library of surrogate policies, which is trained using a hierarchical structure. While our method targets motion planning in dynamic environments, its underlying architecture can be applied to various machine learning domains. We evaluate HPL in a Sliding Tile Puzzle and two navigation tasks. In the Simple Transport RL (STAR) framework, we trained on a multi-agent version of the Traffic Intersection puzzle, demonstrating that HPL outperforms various baseline methods. Furthermore, our training process and the associated surrogate policies in the HPL model for the multi-agent task were published under the open-source **Max** framework.

This paper introduces a management system designed specifically for laboratory data documentation. By eliminating manual data entry and automating processes like documentation, labeling, and archiving, the application aims to minimize human error. Currently, research laboratories predominantly rely on laboratory information management systems (LIMS) for operations. However, these systems are often expensive, proprietary, and features-rich to the point that smaller or mid-sized laboratories—those lacking significant funding—typically cannot justify acquiring them. The proposed application is a straightforward, flexible, and scalable system tailored for institutions of modest to average size. It leverages the open-source programming environment PyQt5, which uses Python, and integrates with the EBI's open-source annotation standard, Recordish, via its implementation of Schema.org. This approach ensures that every piece of data is tagged with specific context, allowing computational tracking from experiment execution through the management of associated assets such as chemicals, materials, and publications. The pyDataLab software performs the essential functions of data entry, documentation, label management, and archiving. These labels, when following Schema.org standards, enable algorithms to understand and contextualize information, facilitating the reconstruction of a research process and a precise replication of its outcomes.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in applying machine learning (ML) and genetic algorithms (GA) to predict and discover new materials. Addressing a critical gap, we introduce an optimized multi-objective optimization approach combined with ML models specifically designed to screen candidate alloys within narrow chemical ranges for manufacturing. We applied this method to a study of high-temperature superalloys, using first-principles data augmented by the SHAP algorithm to predict key properties: melting point, solubility limit, and yield strength. Subsequently, we developed GA to discover the specific alloy composition yielding the most favorable outcomes. Finally, we utilized Pareto optimization and SHAP analysis to identify promising high-performing superalloys, analyzing their underlying mechanisms. We conclude that this integrated methodology offers a robust, efficient approach for selecting optimal material compositions under complex, concurrent constraints.

Extending the AdS/CFT correspondence, we analyze entanglement properties of bulk quantum states that derive from the entropies of boundary states. As boundary entropies satisfy monogamy of mutual information among all entanglement wedges, the same constraint applies to the resulting bulk entropies. Consequently, the bulk quantum states are constrained such that the sum of any set of entanglement wedge entropies surrounding a specific volume must be fixed, allowing the reconstruction of information from the associated mutual information and correcting for quantum contributions.

We investigate a class of solvable lattice models that can be defined through a specific ruleset. Common image-processing practices in astronomy include creating coadded images to boost signal-to-noise ratios and achieve deeper penetrations. Although these methods effectively suppress outliers and systematic artifacts, our investigation reveals that they also induce position-dependent PSF profile variations. Using *ZwI* we examined these effects with *ZwI* simulation stars and found that clipped means and median distributions deviate from a smooth profile, creating a central core that dominates the light distribution. Furthermore, the mean clipped mean shows a clear mismatch between the shape of flux from individual images and that of the coadded result, indicating that for datasets with significant PSF gradient, these nonlinear approaches may distort the final PSF profile.

Quantum verification serves as a pivotal step toward achieving practical quantum computing. While previous models primarily focus on fully or mutually untrusted scenarios, this study presents the first quantum-verification protocol for partially untrusted environments—a setup where the sender (Alice) and receiver (Bob) have differing levels of trust regarding the variational quantum circuit (VQC). Designated as CVQC, this protocol relies on two classical bit strings to verify circuit performance and offers a speed advantage over the current best available method. Additionally, we introduce a second protocol based on quantum channel discrimination, demonstrating that both methods remain robust even if the untrusted component attempts to exploit pre-shared quantum resources.

The rise of deep learning in biomedical imaging has driven a demand for extensive, balanced datasets, yet manual annotation remains prohibitively time-consuming and expert-dependent. To address this, we introduce a deep generative model capable of synthesizing realistic cell shapes that maintains accurate labels, thereby enabling the augmentation of such datasets and enhancement of downstream tasks like cell tracking and segmentation. Our method, named GASS (Gaussian Approximation for cell shape Synthesis), efficiently models anisotropic cell forms using simple ellipses derived from velocity fields. These fields are efficiently learned via stochastic variational inference, facilitating rapid, on-the-fly synthesis. Notably, GASS operates in an end-to-end fashion: it is trained on existing datasets and can simultaneously learn metrics for both data augmentation and the generation of synthetic variations, effectively enhancing dataset utility for downstream analysis.

Building on the success of deep reinforcement learning (RL) across diverse environments, a critical unresolved question remains: which features of an agent's internal representation are essential for successful learning, and can this representation efficiency be enhanced? We investigate this by asking whether specific representation characteristics are linked to performance, including how these relationships might be exploited to extract or distill world models, even across different environments. Measuring the "persistence" of internal states—a property previously shown to underpin generalization—we find a persistent relationship between feature persistence and success in multiple geometric tasks. Specifically, we demonstrate that this connection holds within both single unified settings and undivided contexts. Furthermore, the persistence of these internal states allows for the extraction of latent structural relationships that generalize across various environments. These findings suggest that representation persistence can be harnessed to train robust world models capable of predicting dynamics in both familiar and novel domains.

Using data from the Gaia DR2 catalog, we identify and analyze 1,370 wide binary systems with separations ranging from approximately 1,400 to 10,000 AU. We developed a specific gating strategy to determine the velocity dispersion between these systems and the solar motion, achieving significantly higher precision than previous methods and enabling a more accurate assessment of local kinematics. Our derived dispersion of $0.200 \pm 0.015$ km/s aligns well with earlier studies conducted at lower analytical resolutions. We attribute this improvement to following a systematic procedure that explicitly accounts for potential biases stemming from the mixing of dynamically distinct subpopulations and minimizes errors in determining the systemic radial velocity through the Gaia DR2 net proper motion. Comparatively, we observe that the standard maximum likelihood method applied to tangential and heliocentric velocities yields a dispersion of roughly $1.5\times$ higher than our result using line-of-sight velocities; we conclude that the latter accurately reflects the relative velocities of wide binaries and the local galactic environment.

In this work, we leverage deep learning as a computational approach for detecting the synchronization between matching pairs of time series. Using this method, we can simultaneously map the morphological structure hidden within the raw financial data themselves. While this technique performs exceptionally well on some paired stock series, it fails completely when applied to other pairs, suggesting it effectively either counts or ignores the series' characteristics. Beyond determining synchrony, we also analyze anti-correlation and other relationship types. Ultimately, we have created a new metric: the Time Series Morphology Correlation (TSMC), which serves as an alternative to traditional linear correlation measures.

The discovery of coupling between matter's quantum dynamics and vibrational modes has opened new frontiers in reaction product selectivity and chemical transformation control. This paper examines this interaction from the perspective of quantum information theory, utilizing two-qubit models of tunneling in models modified by one, two, or many vibrational modes. These two quantum states represent the reactant and product, with vibrational excitation on the reaction coordinate, while other modes dissipate energy. Information metrics such as quantum mutual information and quantum discord are found to enhance with the addition of two modes, but mutual information ultimately declines with many modes. Quantizing and analyzing these measures provides insight into non-classical behavior, revealing that mutual information effectively captures the influence of vibrational modes on tunneling. This is further supported by finding that the optimal qubit purity for maximizing quantum discord within a specific decay range corresponds to vibrational excitation. Such unique quantum characteristics may help design reaction barriers that are impossible without vibrational coupling, leading to novel control strategies in chemical reactions.

Accurately predicting the CTR of online advertisements is essential for the effective allocation of web space. This paper presents CTR+NVR, an advanced CTR prediction framework designed to incorporate user, advertiser identities along with session information. Formed for addressing massive multisequential communication issues alongside identity challenges, the model utilizes state-of-the-art large-scale sequence embedding techniques combined with novel strategies to process visual IDs. Specifically, it introduces a direct mapping method to handle visual IDs, which are currently ignored by existing advertising session models. By effectively integrating signals from both user and advertiser identities, the model enhances the learning of comprehensive user and advertiser profiles. Extensive experiments conducted across major industry datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently surpasses current baseline methods by a significant margin.

This paper explores the integration of cardinality constraints into business process management (BPM). While these constraints successfully model cardinality and parity rules vital for business logic, their implementation introduces intricate dependencies between events that either synchronize or compete for resources. Such interactions complicate the handling of concurrent processes and create challenges for the temporal ordering of events. To address this, the authors model the dependency graph associated with cardinality constraints, analyzing properties that ensure graph connectivity and account for work remaining on tasks. They outline specific instances instantiating work estimates using upper and lower bounds, a feature demonstrated by its validity across interval temporal networks. Finally, the authors derive implications for temporal interface definitions, process validity assessment, and algorithmic soundness.

Although conditionally dependent data is prevalent in nature, existing privacy-preserving frameworks for location-based service (LBS) queries typically overlook the potential for privacy erosion caused by such dependencies. This study introduces a new, comprehensive privacy framework that not only considers direct identification risk but also addresses potential re-identification through conditionally dependent information. This system utilizes a privacy similarity metric based on "t-distance"—the minimum travel distance between two users— to quantify the level of protection required against t-distance-related linkage attacks. Aligned with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mandates the consideration of all reasonable inference possibilities, we examine three distinct user scenarios: (1) users whose profiles contain no externally linked information, (2) users already protected against inference risks from other data sources, and (3) users possessing other data that could be used for inference. By analyzing these contexts, we derived closed-form mathematical formulas for the privacy similarity metric and formulated a generalized question of whether a specific user violates a given privacy threshold. Finally, we evaluated the framework using real-world taxi datasets to demonstrate its practicality and effectiveness.

Inter-site variations in functional connectivity (FC) hold significant value for distinguishing between individuals and identifying disease-related changes. However, it remains unclear to what extent these effects persist after accounting for strong inter-site correlations inherent in standard FC metrics, such as those between area V1 and V2. We analyzed the relationship between site pairs across the MIND dataset using two approaches: the raw correlation of their time series (standard FC) and the correlation of their signal power spectrum densities (PSW), which removes high-frequency components. By examining the distribution of these connectivity values for all 795 area pair combinations, we found the median and 95th percentile values normalized across subjects; these normalized scores were then converted to z-values for further analysis. Our results demonstrate that after flattening the signal, both the mean and variability of the estimated z-FC are reduced, thereby diminishing the influence of high-frequency noise. Consequently, the correlation estimates become more reliable, making the detection of between-group and inter-subject variations easier. Applying this high-frequency filtering yields FC estimates that reveal increased sensitivity to fine-grained differences. These findings suggest that filtering out high-frequency components in pre-processing enhances the utility of FC for high-resolution studies of functional organization and variability.

This study offers additional applications derived from our recent solution to the optimal constant in the Talagrand concentration of measure inequality for the Gaussian measure, which is characterized by a dual formulation based on the $L^2$-Wasserstein metric. We apply this approach to address two specific problems: in analysis, we determine the sharp constant for the Brascamp-Hirsch inequality during $\delta$-entropic interpolation and resolve the optimal constant for the Boltzmann entropy, established via the logarithmic Sobolev constant in Gaussian space; within probability theory, we derive refined inequalities for both the Baumgartner and Székely formulations related to $\delta$-entropic interpolation.

This paper investigates positional encoding strategies to enable language models to process code-mixed text. The proposed positional encodings are integrated into the pre-trained multi-classification model CONEXT by next, which was pre-trained using the multilingual Next Sentence and Next Word datasets. Results show that these techniques perform on par with or better than the existing positional encodings that were developed specifically for multi-language NLP tasks. Furthermore, the proposed encodings surpass an approach that utilizes separate self-attention layers to handle different languages, especially in the context of the most complex language mix scenarios. Finally, the techniques demonstrate effectiveness across various two-language combinations, including Latin-Devanagari and Latin-Greek.

Substitution effects are central to multiple research areas in biology, including gene prioritization, gene-phenotype mapping, and evolutionary analysis. However, a single genetic substitution influences an extensive network of interacting processes, creating feedback loops that generate a spectrum of potential effects ranging from minor to major. Because these dimensions represent distinct biological realities, no single metric can be considered the "correct" or "true" effect. This work derives analytical results to determine how different dimensions of a gene's effects map to phenotypic changes, revealing that average impacts correlate with elevated downstream activity, whereas sensitivity-specific phenotypic changes are driven primarily by signals that pass through system bottlenecks. To test these theoretical findings, we utilized whole-cell mathematical models to simulate whole organism phenotypes and validated our predictions through both model and gene-set-enrichment analyses, thereby confirming our framework in a biologically realistic environment.

This study introduces a novel energy optimization strategy for bipedal robots that integrates closed-loop control systems with dynamic programming. Distinct from standard optimization approaches reliant on open-loop trajectories and zero net energy flow over gait cycles, this method utilizes experimentally measured gait cycle durations as historical data. By treating these past gait cycles as a reference, future steps are planned to accumulate a total net energy flow close to zero, effectively balancing energy consumption throughout the walking sequence. This technique depends on two key components: a feedback-controlled bipedal robot and a backward-pass dynamic programming (BDP) algorithm. The robustness of this closed-loop BDP method was validated through experiments involving a 20-kg, 10-degree-of-freedom (DoF) human-scale robot, comparing results against both an open-pass version and an open-loop BDC implementation.

This paper examines camera pose estimation using only five key points, a practical choice for real-world applications that balances robustness and efficiency. While this task is generally reliable, we identify specific difficult scenarios where current methods fail. Rather than focusing on these difficult cases, we propose a novel strategy using learned descriptors to refine pose estimates. This approach involves jointly training the descriptors and a nearest neighbor solver, with a particular emphasis on modifying the solver to prioritize in-scene points and effectively bypass out-scene points and outliers. While this method is universally applicable to any rich descriptor set, it is evaluated here with LAPHONET. Results across both synthetic and real-world datasets are analyzed, and we conclude that this new strategy significantly improves the robustness of pose estimation.

Personalized federated learning (PFL) aims to establish distinct local models for each client, differing both from the global model and from other individual clients. In this research, we investigate semi-supervised PFL by incorporating unlabelled data into the learning process. We present a novel approach that utilizes the pseudo-labels of these unlabeled instances to enhance personalization. Specifically, the method constructs a distillation target, guided by the predictions of a shared teacher model, with the goal of improving the performance of clients who have label limitations. The resulting framework is designed to boost individual customization for clients with few labels while maintaining robust personalization for those with abundant labeled data. Empirical evaluations on several benchmark data sets confirm the method's efficiency, delivering substantial gains in label-scarce scenarios and competitive results otherwise. The implementation is available at: https://github.com/MLSPYY/PseudoDistiPFL.

Under weak conditions on the generator, this work establishes the existence of a unique quasi-stationary distribution featuring exponential decay, describes the conditional behavior of the complementary event, and demonstrates asymptotic independence within the living region. In this study, we establish a theoretical framework to examine equilibrium and dynamical states of dielectric objects interacting with both graphene-based jets of radiation and non-relativistic photons. Specifically, we analyze how varying the chemical potential of the graphene changes particle equilibrium locations; a non-zero chemical potential shifts all centers of gravity away from the two-dimensional carbonsheet. Additionally, we compute the Acoustic Casimir effect by considering a one-rank dielectric slab suspended by radiative graphene on both sides, and by considering a dielectric rod partially embedded within a graphene channel on the surface.

Even though length of stay in the Emergency Department (ED) serves as a primary metric for gaaging hospital efficiency, the impact of patient wait time on overall length of stay has not been conclusively measured. The concept of "realized wait time" is defined as the sum of an individual's actual waiting period and the median delay experienced by their peer group. The study presented utilizes a difference-in-differences approach to determine causal relationships, demonstrating that a 30-minute increase in ED volume leads to higher levels of returns and readmissions within 30 days. Furthermore, while increased pressure does extend the time patients remain in the hospital, it simultaneously allows more individuals to depart within 24 hours. Notably, these efficiency and flow benefits are most pronounced for patients with minimal acuity.

This research investigates the Wittfeld and colleagues' conjecture, specifically analyzing how the distribution of task difficulties shapes the optimal approach to problem-solving by single agents and optimal coordination methods across groups. We provide proof that the authors original proposal holds true for every task difficulty distribution. Furthermore, while a strictly monotonic difficulty level requires a simple strategy, non-strict cases allow for diverse optimal methods; however, the most optimal strategies effectively utilize task information in both sophisticated and rudimentary ways. In the context of strictly stochastic difficulties, we demonstrate that the desired procedure corresponds precisely to the proposed solution. In the final section, we broaden the framework to incorporate agents' capacity for mutual communication.

This study introduces a decentralized learning technique for deep neural networks that enables multiple organizations to jointly train models for intrusions without sharing their private data. By utilizing an iterative update approach based on stochastic gradient descent, the proposed method allows participants to remain privacy-preserving while still contributing to global model development. The system is also adaptable to scenarios involving the training of distinct deep learning architectures. Experimental results across three real-world datasets demonstrate a result that is comparable to training performed on a single, centralized dataset, and confirms the method's efficiency in scenarios with multiple organizations.

We introduce a new parallelism-aware scheduling algorithm designed specifically for robustly executing time-critical, real-world robotic tasks. While existing scheduling strategies are often too simplistic to handle the complex, time-constrained applications found in robotics, our approach treats these scenarios as periodic tasks on a shared platform to provide a practical and user-friendly solution. By leveraging a specific model of the robotic applications, our algorithm efficiently and accurately predicts the optimal level of parallelism. This dynamic adjustment of parallelness is core to our method: during low-load periods, it minimizes the use of parallel resources to handle execution, and during busy periods, it rapidly escalates parallelism to ensure tasks meet their deadlines. We validate the effectiveness and robustness of this dynamic parallelism management through extensive experiments. These tests cover everything from basic robotic movements to complex, multi-day science protocols actually used at the International Space Station, highlighting our algorithm's superior performance.

"Advancements in device architecture and materials are essential for continuing progress in silicon technology toward miniaturization. Specifically, transitioning from thermal silicon dioxide to high-k gate dielectrics was a pivotal milestone. Nevertheless, contact resistance at the metal/high-k interface remains worse than that at the silicon/high-k interface, causing the mobility benefits of the new dielectric to be negated. Therefore, improving contact resistance is now a critical objective. Our research proposes analyzing various metal and high-k material combinations to study how these factors influence the contact resistance. Findings indicate that the Al2O3/HfZrO4 (HfZrO) and high-Al metal from the CASM 21 group offer the most promising pathways to lowering contact resistance. Our recommended configurations are poised to significantly advance future technological node achievements."

This study evaluates how network performance depends on the size of parameters and initial conditions. Specifically, it investigates whether asymptotic synchronization can emerge in networks featuring slightly mismatched oscillators. By extending prior work on the mean convergence of stochastic systems, we demonstrate that for systems with homogeneous mean coupling, if the synchronization manifold is asymptotically stable, then for networks with inhomogeneous coupling, this manifold remains conditionally stable. This conditional stability holds even when parameter variations are small, with the upper limit for this tolerance level decreasing as the degree of mismatch increases. Furthermore, we generalize the use of the small-gain theorem to prove the conditional asymptotic stability of a cluster formed by $m$ distinct synchronization manifolds.

In a conformal theory without defects, the $\zeta$-function is simply evaluated using the standard spectrum of holomorphic and anti-holomorphic generators ($V$ and $A$). This path-dependency is characterized by a $\zeta$-function derived from a set of matrices representing the action of defects on that operator content. Network protocols are analyzed as mechanisms that auto-regulate delay and bandwidth to align with specific requirements. This work examines how these protocols auto-regulate based on locally measured delay, which may include a fixed component, and demonstrates that multiple distinct operational regimes—characterized by different delay splits between the fixed component and alignment with requirements—can coexist. An external measurement model for delay is established, after which the dynamics are linearized and analyzed for stability. The stability behaviors reveal that not all regimes are equally stable. We introduce the concept of local-functional learning to address domain adaptation in settings with minimal data. Features from pre-trained models, such as ResNet, are frequently employed to enhance downstream tasks through transfer learning. The concept of Accretion-Induced Collapse (AIC) describes an accretion-driven process where a white dwarf (WD) transforms into a neutron star. We present a general approach for computing specific types of first integrals for higher-order Euler-Lagrange differential equations, with applications extending to complex models like the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator.

To demonstrate the power of this framework, we identify multiple families of first integrals for the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator of arbitrary order and apply the method to various higher-order models found in cosmology.

This study examines a fluid that is not perfect (i.e., possesses non-vanishing viscosity and heat conductivity) and spherically symmetric. Using a global causal framework to analyze these singular solutions, the study reveals that any complete extension necessitates an event horizon, a surface whose area can be calculated. The proof proceeds by perturbation: starting from the well-established scenario where an initially finite-profile mass distribution leads to a null, inextendible singularity, the analysis examines the effect of adding small disturbances to that mass distribution. The findings indicate two distinct outcomes: the nature of the singhide—whether it remains exposed or becomes concealed—depends critically on whether the initial mass distribution was "close to being constant." Specifically, the geometry of the resulting event horizon varies based on this "proximity." While certain perturbations leave the singhide unchanged (leading to a null singhide), other small perturbations generate a timelike event hide, with the singular surface's area determined by characteristics of both the original mass profile and the perturbation itself.

Recent advancements in reinforcement learning have seen the integration of intrinsic motivation to enhance exploration, often yielding successful results; yet, a critical examination of its impact on training compared to using only extrinsic rewards remains missing. Neuromorphic systems are emerging as a high-throughput, low-power alternative to traditional computer architectures. To support rapid and cost-effective design iterations, it is essential to deploy a reliable hardware simulation environment. However, due to the immense scale of these platforms, minimizing simulation time remains a significant obstacle. Recent studies have indicated that reducing simulation speed requires decoupling hardware components, and this degree of separation varies depending on the chosen virtual platform architecture. This paper investigates the impact of four distinct architecture designs on neuromorphic simulations, measuring the performance of each to identify which yields the fastest results. Findings reveal that a fully coupled model incurs the least speed penalty in current conditions; yet, as future simulators become more optimized, the advantage of the fully coupled approach is expected to diminish.

This paper proposes In-decision Trees, a new structure that extends traditional decisions with confidence estimates. This study examines the performance enhancement of time series similarity search that results from "early abandoning" during the comparison process. Since the quality of early abandonment is tied to the accuracy of delay time estimation, we evaluate various estimation methods and propose a new technique. This study analyzes the impact of automated feedback on student problem sets, specifically examining three intervention types: line-by-line reports, coverage-based summaries, and no feedback at all. Intermingled groups of 64 first-year computer science students participated in 10 programming exercises over a semester, each followed by a failed submission and a final successful submission. We collected 184 in-process submissions and used a design-of-experiments approach to assess the effects of the feedback conditions on code progress, completeness, and academic grades. Results indicate the feedback's format significantly influences student performance and submission strategies. While line-by-line details frequently prompt unnecessary code alterations, we found that students receiving such messages achieve lower final scores compared to those without such detailed instructions. Conversely, we observed that providing summary feedback—rather than none at all, and using a line-free format—correlates with higher grades and leads to more efficient solutions with higher code coverage.

Understanding the rationale behind decisions made by black-box classifiers remains a significant challenge. Previous approaches to explaining these decisions primarily fall into two categories: (1) generating local interpretations by perturbing specific inputs for an individual decision, and (2) decomposing global classifications by modifying input features statistically. This work proposes an alternative framework that produces symbolic surrogate models as global explanations. These models aim to mimic a target classifier by relying on other feature-based rules. We address both accuracy and robustness by seeking and leveraging symbolic models for explaining decisions. Specifically, we train these models to maintain a certain statistical independence, which not only improves predictive performance but also yields simpler interpretations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the search for such symbolic surrogates uncovers which features drive decisions and which remain irrelevant.

Building on these findings, the paper presents a new method that achieves competitive transitive classification (CC) and node classification tasks. Experimental results on thirteen real-world datasets show that the number of layers in this new method can be increased significantly, including up to ten times more layers in some cases compared to standard KNN-SGC.

A newly developed, automatic common trends estimator is introduced; it relies on bandwidth selection and functions by counting the dimension of eigenvalues falling below a specific threshold. Infrastructure investment by internet service providers (ISPs) is essential for enabling global cache distribution and ensuring rapid content delivery. Phys.* **88**, 644–650, 2020), this article extends the non-standard quantization of a system's kinetic and potential energies, proposed here a decade prior. That earlier model modeled hydrogen's stability and the Balmer series, requiring only classical, non-random energy dissipation. In this updated formulation, we treat kinetic and potential energies of a two-body system as following a two-state Markov random walk, simulated efficiently using the Gibbs sampling algorithm over two discrete states. This results in a Brownian-like motion for the electrons and, through the conservation of total energy, specific spectral lines. The key distinction from prior models is a dynamic, energy-exchange mechanism between the radiation and the atom. This approach achieves the same spectral outcomes through real, stochastic energy dissipation. Liger is an open-source Python framework designed for large-scale, collaborative scientific computations on petascale supercomputers, developed and maintained by an international collective of scientists and engineers with extensive code documentation and software released under open licenses. Liger relies on two essential components: (1) the Data Reduction System (DRS), which handles in situ and offline data transformations, and (2) the I/O Management System (IMS), which facilitates the construction of adaptive, multi-layer output architectures to distribute both transient and permanent datasets. This paper specifically addresses the DRS as the primary contribution, a system realized through the PhoeniExase simulation, a high-fidelity, three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model of in-situ combustion within coal seams. Operating as the second largest active simulation utilizing Liger on the Apollonian supercomputing cluster, it was deployed to validate the framework's capabilities. This computational experiment investigates the complex, coupled spatial and temporal interactions of thermal, fluid, and chemical processes while simultaneously stress-testing the pipeline for handling the storage and processing of petabyte-scale datasets.

Findings indicate that a substantial portion of patients underwent ICU admission without necessarily exhibiting a clear progression of viral infection. This insight underscores the necessity of ICU resources and supports a real-time, prognostic application of both clustering and GMM methods, potentially guiding more strategic resource use. Additionally, we introduce specific clinical pathway metrics designed to benchmark future COVID-19 trials, an effort further enhanced by integrating recent public datasets, which will facilitate the clinical translation of our discoveries.

This study tackles the challenge of propagating timing delays in Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCC) circuits. First, it proposes a novel technique for MCC implementation by leveraging constant relationship data to enable parallel operation, which significantly improves circuit performance compared to approaches that ignore these constants. Second, a design tool specifically developed to support this implementation strategy is detailed. This tool incorporates proposed error propagation mechanisms into a static timing analysis to more accurately calculate the circuit's skew and delay. The effectiveness of this method is verified through a comparative analysis of previously synthesized MCC circuits, highlighting that the error-aware timing model correctly identifies the impact of component variations. Ultimately, this error propagation is critical for: (1) accurately predicting the total MCC circuit delay; (2) reducing delay in applications where constant relationships are exploited; and (3) enabling designers to prioritize delay-critical paths.

While machine learning achieves remarkable success across numerous fields, the field of quantum deep learning currently faces significant research challenges. This study introduces a novel quantum architecture based on the Bayesian network. The model demonstrates efficacy in both classification and regression tasks and enhances the interpretability of neural networks through quantum probabilistic inference. Furthermore, the implementation of this structure on an actual quantum processor holds the potential to reveal intrinsic characteristics of deep quantum circuits that current experimental data has thus far obscured.

Natural language parsing involves constructing a tree structure that reflects the hierarchical relations within a sentence. Historically, this required complex, manually engineered grammatical rules, but recent advances have shifted towards using neural network parsers that learn these structures from annotated data. However, the parsing models developed this way rely on these annotations for the target language itself and transfer poorly to languages with zero or limited labels. Previously, cross-lingual parsing was only feasible for language pairs that share annotated parsing trees. We have previously proposed FPIO, a novel few-shot parsing framework that learns hierarchical relations for a target language using only a minimal set of annotated trees. We further develop this approach by proposing PFIO, which allows the model to initially learn a universal cross-lingual representation of hierarchical relations by training on multiple source languages before parsing. Specifically, we find that PFIO, when trained with just three or ten marked constituent trees, can produce high-precision parse trees for a target language. This performance significantly and consistently surpasses that of standard zero-shot or most current few-shot natural language parsing techniques and is also comparable to the results obtained by models trained on just one annotated tree. Finally, we also explore the use of parsing models in this setup for low-resource NLP tasks, such as natural language inference and natural language semantic parsing, with findings indicating that few-shot semantically parsed structures can effectively enhance the performance of natural language semantic parsing models and inference systems trained with limited data.

This study re-examines the skin effect within non-Hermitian systems, utilizing an extended Hatano-Nelson model to reveal a distinct connection between entanglement and this phenomenon. While non-Hermitian chains typically exhibit an anisotropic skin-effect expansion that can be strengthened by correlations, we find that at a specific non-Hermitian parameter value, the effect vanishes completely. This is because the system transitions into a state of maximized quantum entanglement, forming a maximally entangled quantum state. We propose that the presence of the skin effect stems from localized non-Hermitian chains possessing low or absent entanglement, and we view the vanishing of the effect as a special instance within a broader transition to high entangality. The subsequent analysis of a non-Hermitian Rydberg many-body lattice reinforces this theoretical framework, suggesting that the non-Hermitian skin effect and entanglement are intrinsically linked. We anticipate these insights will advance the understanding of the skin effect in various non-Hermitian systems.

The analysis of multi-particle scattering in planar $N=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory utilizes an generalized version of the factorized scattering amplitude for non-abelian currents. Pulsar halos, comprising dispersed plasma and cosmic rays generated by pulsar wind interactions with their surrounding magnetic fields, are now prominent in models explaining both the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess observed by FERMI-LAT and the positron surplus detected on Earth. While the precision measurements by H.E.S.S. hint at a渊源 for the GeV gamma-ray background, conventional halo representations often fail to replicate this data because they predict a nearly flat GeV spectrum, which does not align with the required spectral features; consequently, it remains uncertain whether the halo mechanism itself can fully account for both excesses. We demonstrate that for a fixed cosmic ray injection profile, the resulting diffuse emission spectrum is profoundly sensitive to the spatial distribution parameters of the halos. Our findings reveal a powerful capability in pulsar halo emission to bridge the spectral gap between the two phenomena. Specifically, a previously unpublished injection schema successfully reproduces the required spectral signature for the TeV excess while remaining consistent with observations from the GeV band, including potential explanations for the Galactic Center F-GLAST data. Additionally, this schema produces a calculated TeV sky map where emission is tightly bound to visible pulsar locations, characterized by a resolved point-source distribution rather than a smooth background.

Conventional methods for increasing the quantity of training data often yield limited gains in convoluted neural network (CNN) performance. This study explores a fresh strategy that leverages delimiting superpixel masks to augment image datasets, with the objective of improving CNN performance and mitigating overfitting. This approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios with scarce data, such as the training of a single CNN. The proposed solution involves a new set of unsupervised features designed to delineate semantically distinct regions within an image, effectively identifying regions of interest. These features are then harnessed to generate corresponding superpixel delimitation masks, which can either expand existing datasets or, when combined with the original information (and potentially other transformed or unlabeled variations), strengthen a dataset. The results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms established techniques in visual classification, including natural and medical image categorization.

To date, there is a lack of understanding regarding the types of scientific research on general topics that attract policymakers' attention. Using a database of U.S. federal activities between 2007 and 2017, we apply text-matching techniques alongside AI-driven advancements to trace government policy interests across various scientific disciplines. Sentence quality classification (SQC) is a critical natural language processing task that supports various downstream applications. In this study, we explore and benchmark the use of Wikipedia editing patterns to enhance SQM models. While a recent approach suggested leveraging an editor's previous actions to predict what a single contributor might do next, we observe that these editing patterns yield even greater benefits by directly improving the labeling process itself. Based on this insight, we introduce **EditSQI_Suggest**, a system that enhances SQM performance by incorporating features derived from editing behaviors. Experiments conducted on the Robust04 benchmark set with our best method achieve a **F1 score of 79.33%**, representing an **9.33% absolute improvement** (or a total gain of nearly 1 percentage point improvement relative to prior baselines) compared to the 71.81% F1 score of a standard non-trained linear model.

We evaluate DB3's efficacy in two distinct contexts: first, a real-world black-box attack on Graph Neural Networks, demonstrating its potential to bridge gaps in model capabilities; and, proposed works target a state-of-the-art large language model. To advance capabilities further in both scenarios, we combine DB3 with an iterative refinement strategy, enabling continuous improvement through multiple query cycles to teachers.

This work addresses two primary challenges: (1) identifying networks where interference exists, and (2) finding the optimal, non-interfering focal units to include in an experiment, both using only interferenced group outcomes. We address these by creating a class of tests that are robust to interference within the groups but remain valid when the selection of individual focal units follows either an independent or mutually independent identically distributed (m.i.i.d.) distribution. Our methods apply to both continuous and censored treatment levels, assuming a selection process driven by maximizing treatment utility. The tests function by comparing the observed treatment response mean in a setting with any interference against a synthetic no-interference benchmark, with this benchmark also possessing a valid no-interference property. We demonstrate that using multiple focal units improves the ability to detect interference, and that our proposed choices for this benchmark generally perform better in practice. Finally, the specific test statistics and the method for choosing focal units are publicly available on GitHub at a dedicated repository (https://github.com/andrewjzhu1/UtilityFWPT).

This work investigates the impact of interacting dark matter (DM) within neutron stars, specifically focusing on scenarios where DM self-annihilations contribute to stellar cooling. While prior studies have established conditions for DM stability, they often overlooked the complex interaction between this retained matter and the star's thermal mechanisms. This research addresses two critical aspects: first, it quantifies the mass range of dark matter capable of reaching a self-sustaining equilibrium, and second, it calculates the resulting temperature profile of the neutron star during its cooling phase while incorporating DM annihilation. The calculations reveal a sensitive dependence of the central temperature on both the DM density and the annihilation rate. Consequently, detecting a mid-age neutron star with an abnormally low central temperature could provide compelling evidence for the presence of stable, annihilation-capable dark matter within its core.

Experimental validation on three public datasets—including two newly created sparse- focused ones—demonstrates that these user representations significantly outperform those from other leading document-based models. Chaotic scattering with infinite Wada basins presents a striking example of a boundary phenomenon where three or more domains each share a common, completely dense frontier. In this investigation, we analyze such a configuration under ultrasmall dissipative inflow. The numerical simulations reveal that for a small number of trials, the Wada property remains intact across all basin categories. However, as simulation lengths grow toward infinity, dissipative effects fragment the basins, eliminating certain infinite regions while augmenting others. Notably, the largest growth is observed in the smallest basins, which exhibit a dramatic increase in scale. Furthermore, we investigate how altering the system's smoothness impacts these dynamics. Specifically, reducing smoothness to non-integer orders via fractional differential equations triggers a bifurcation point in the system parameters. Above this critical threshold, the fractal dimensions of the resulting basin boundaries shift abruptly.

We propose a low-energy photon collider concept designed to target the muon g-2 anomaly parameter space, with significant potential for being implemented at DESY's NLCC (Next Light Colliders) facility. Our analysis shows that even a very low-energy configuration, specifically a 200 MeV NLCC, can identify many dark photon models intended to explain the g-2 discrepancy. Furthermore, while higher-energy collarts offer broader discovery reach for both the dark photon and dark matter, a virtual photon beam paired with conventional e+e- collisions enables precise measurements of the produced dark matter. This approach allows NLCs to achieve a detailed understanding of hidden sector models explaining the muon g-2 mystery, even with particles that are inherently inaccessible via direct production methods.

Human Video Understanding involves addressing complex cognitive tasks, where the brain plays a key role in identifying significant areas within video frames and temporal changes, even when dealing with incomplete information. This paperintroduces HAN, a novel hierarchical architecture inspired by these human mechanisms. HAN employs a multi-step spatial-temporal attention mechanism that identifies crucial regions across consecutive frames and temporal dimensions. This approach is deeply rooted in neuro-biological processes: (1) visual areas (V1-V4) excel at extracting basic features from raw video, (2) the inferior parietal and prefrontal cortex organize these features into local objects, and ( (3) the brain then selectively focuses on significant areas. This process mirrors the proposed hierarchical attention modules. This three-tiered framework (brain, object, attention) enables HAN to effectively identify key regions, analyze hierarchies, and recognize objects. This model has been applied to human-centered video understanding tasks, including human pose estimation, action recognition, and identifying important parts in both images and videos. This paper demonstrates that HAN achieves superior results compared to existing leading methods across these specific benchmarks.

This investigation examines how scattered energy behaves within the contexts of scalar field scattering and information paradoxes at both extremal and near-extremal black hole conditions. In the absence of an ADM mass bound, scattering events near the extremal limit yield extreme final states that serve as nearly ideal counterparts to the canonical split between extremality deviation and black hole mass. However, the absence of such a bound results in nearly ideal outcomes regardless of the initial approach to extremality. While the near-extremal case without the mass bound produces a physically meaningful black hole, the strictly extremal case typically yields a scalar cloud—a non-black-hole configuration. The transition to a scalar cloud is particularly sensitive to the degree of non-extremality, occurring within an approximately $10^{-6}$ window. Moreover, the metric exhibits distinct behaviors: it approaches the standard Reissner-Nordström geometry as parameters stay within the valid range, yet diverges significantly from the expected form in the presence of a scalar cloud.

Video analysis is a powerful method for examining human life, yet interpreting content—particularly tiny moving objects—is computationally challenging. While current models often mimic non-biological motion, this work focuses on distinguishing biological from non-biological entities. We present the first end-to-dedeep-learning framework capable of modeling generalizable characteristics of general biological motion derived from video. We demonstrate that using two new proposed components, the **Embedding of general biological motion (EBM)** and the **Flow-based biological prior (FBP)** effectively capture distinct biological motion patterns. FBM encodes static characteristics, while FBP models dynamic kinematics. FBP achieves this by training a neural network to encode specific biological movement profiles and organizing them into a generative framework based on biological flow. We validate FBP's generative capabilities and biological specificity using two test suites: a classification of different animal walking styles and the prediction of missing video frames. We conclude by discussing future applications and uses of this technique.

Furthermore, we evaluated this algorithm within a microgrid context by addressing the problem of strategic network reconfiguration.

This research examines the evolutionary processes behind spiral galaxy warps, specifically investigating the contrasting origins of S-type (forward accelerating) and U-type (reverse accelerating) warps. By analyzing observations from the Legacy Extragalactic Radio Structure Survey (LEGRESS) and comparing the results with N-body simulations, the study explores the evolutionary trajectories of both warp types. LEGRESS data reveals that S-type warps are associated with strong tidal forces, close encounters, and frequent interactions with nearby galaxy groups or clusters. In contrast, the central disks of U-type warped galaxies exhibit higher specific angular momentum and a lower circular velocity dispersion, indicating that their formation is less tied to interactions. Simulations further confirm that S-type warps result from interactions, showing that a disc tilted toward its circumgalactic medium (CGM) and accompanied by a negative (S-type) warp angle is the stable outcome when a system experiences either one or multiple encounters. Conversely, u-type warps arise in scenarios where a disc is already surrounded by a halo possessing high angular momentum. Furthermore, while the two warp types are present across all mass ranges, LEGRESS data shows that S-type warps are significantly more common in low-mass galaxies, a trend that interacts with the mass distribution of nearby neighbors. Finally, the findings suggest that the two warp types are often complementary, suggesting that the complete, large-scale asymmetric structures encompassing both types may offer critical insights into the circumgalactic medium and the intergalactic medium.

Magnetic monopoles, predicted by quantum mechanics in the 1970s, recently moved from theoretical possibility to near-experimental reality due to the discovery of strong magnetoelectric coupling in smectic multiferroics. This coupling means that electric effects can induce magnetization and, dually, magnetic fields can induce polarization. A prominent consequence of this interaction is the Witten effect, where magnetic monopoles acquire an electric charge proportional to the field strength. Conversely, inducing a magnetic dipole within an electric environment serves as a unique signature for observing multiferroic properties. However, investigating dipoles presents specific difficulties, as the energy associated with magnetic interactions of single dipoles is roughly nine orders of magnitude smaller than the energy resulting from the interaction of two dipoles in close proximity. To address the detection of these faint signals, we employed a magnetoelectric resonator operating at microwave frequencies. By coupling this resonator to a superconducting quantum interference detector, we were able to reveal an exceptionally weak rotational energy shift of 500 Hz in smectic multiferroic single crystals, corresponding to magnetically induced polarization. This observation confirms that our setup can detect the theoretically predicted magnetoelectric effect.

This estimate is assumed to remain valid as long as the system remains stable, allowing for early estimation of modal number before conducting a specific eigenvalue analysis to determine system stability, as the prior rough estimate aids in deciding whether a specific reduced order model technique is applicable based on expected system behavior.

This paper introduces an innovative, cost-effective method for road condition monitoring that leverages the smartphones already carried by commuters. By automatically capturing and analyzing road images through these devices, the system identifies and classifies road markings, all while accounting for the unpredictable varying angles introduced by different mobile users. This work details the development of a dedicated Android application facilitating simple image acquisition, which then undergoes server-side processing and analysis. The system was initially validated using a dataset of 4,400 manually annotated images collected from ten streets in South Korea. Additionally, successful real-world trials confirmed the approach's potential, proving successful with 160 image sets gathered during on-the-go tests involving 12 different streets in Italy.

In recent years, imitation learning has seen significant progress, with numerous methods emerging to tackle diverse tasks; however, most research assumes a perfect match between the mathematical models of both the expert and the student. This study investigates a gap frequently found in practical applications, where an environmental discrepancy exists between the data collection phase and execution. Whether due to hardware shifts, software changes, or varying starting and boundary conditions, such a mismatch makes previous ideal approaches inapplicable. Motivated by this reality, the authors present a new reward-free reinforcement learning algorithm that overcomes these challenges without relying on any reward function. By first translating the offset present in observational pairs to a rotation and a goal projection, the method projects the observations and targets into a new space, effectively overcoming the environmental disparity. In a proof, the study shows that the policy generated is asymptotically optimal in the worst-case scenario, supported by a demonstrated computational performance on a new robotic imitation learning benchmark.

This study utilizes the PHANTOM project to analyze angular momentum evolution in a sample of 12 T Tauri stars, white dwarfs, and brown dwarfs, relying on data from protostellar accretion rates ($\dot{M}_{*}$) and circumstellar accretion disc properties—including radii ($R_{\rm{disc}}$), viscosity ($\alpha$), and $\dot{M}_{\rm{disc}}$)—to reconstruct circumstellar angular momentum ($L_{\rm{env}}$) during protostar formation. The findings indicate that discs are consistently unable to absorb the environment's angular momentum protostellarily; consequently, most star formation scenarios necessitate additional mechanisms, specifically magnetic braking, acting on infalling material. Moreover, we demonstrate that an almighty angular momentum can predict star formation outcomes, notably disk fragmentation. Systems characterized by exceptionally low angular momentum fail to fragment, producing star clusters, whereas high angular momentum facilitates fragment formation, potentially generating multiple star systems. Finally, we estimate the fraction of direct protostellar envelope accretion to total protostellar accretion and explore detectability via the millimeter-wave regime.

Association rules are fundamental because of their simplicity, ease of interpretation, and broad application. This paper examines redundancy by framing association analysis as a form of concept or term extraction. A key finding indicates that much apparent rule redundancy stems from logical relationships; specifically, terms like "children" are more specific than "adults," and "white" is more specific than "other." This distinction explains why the rule "other, other" is logically distinct from, and does not duplicate "other, other."

To address this, a framework based on partial order theory defines a rule $B \cup A$ as redundant if it is logically entailment by another, meaning its components are already captured without adding informational value. This reduces understanding and characterizing many instances of redundancy to analyzing logical entailment. The authors propose a novel algorithm that performs this task in $O(n^2)$ time, where $n$ represents the number of attributes. Additionally, they introduce a term-specific partial order and its corresponding equivalence relation, which can be applied to detect and manage redundant terms, thereby solving the redundancy issue in association rules.

Addressing the rising threat of violence stemming from untreated mental disorders, this research investigates whether analyzing patterns in historical crime reports offers a pathway to forecasting future offenses. We collected and anonymized approximately 99,000 crime records from the Chicago Police Department spanning a decade, then developed recurrent neural network models to evaluate if these behavioral sequences can predict specific future crimes. Our results reveal that certain offenses, particularly those related to drugs and mental health, follow distinctive sequence patterns. By leveraging this knowledge, we successfully reduced recidivism prediction errors related to drug and mental health crimes by 25% and 15% as standalone models. Additionally, we developed "treatment-adjusted" models that incorporate historical treatment data; these improved prediction accuracy another 15% for drug-related and 12% for mental health incidents in a multi-task setting. Analysis of these models highlights the critical role these crimes play in predicting subsequent violence. Finally, integrating direct treatment history with the identified crime patterns yielded an additional recidivism prediction boost of 16% for drug cases and 5% for mental health cases via the multi-task approach.

This paper investigates a decentralized learning framework for estimating radio maps, accounting for sources such as inter-antenna channel variations and the stochastic nature of the radio environment. The proposed scheme utilizes a map representation that maintains local estimation states at each node, generated by integrating previous updates with newly acquired data. A map uncertainty metric is then implemented to guide the optimization of the sampling process; specifically, it predicts future observation locations, which are then rounded to the nearest feasible grid point. The core challenge of online parameter updating is addressed by developing an adaptive step-size strategy. Furthermore, the approach enables fully decentralized data processing, as it relies exclusively on local information and neighbor interactions. Simulation results demonstrate that this method requires a significantly lower number of sensors than existing techniques to achieve a specified estimation accuracy.

Modern machine learning models, particularly those trained using algorithms like representation and contrastive learning in representations, can effectively identify out-of-distribution samples through their learned structures. Since these models capture the characteristics of in-distribution samples within their data representations, they naturally flag anomalies as deviations from this pattern. Consequently, the continuous learning of normal characteristics allows these models to detect anomalies in a fully unsupervised manner, eliminating the cost and effort usually associated with labeling anomaly data. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of how various unsupervised and self-supervised learning models function as anomaly detectors. We evaluate both the strengths and limitations of each approach and anoint the specific scenarios where they excel. Our findings include a simple yet efficient method that leverages a pre-trained model, developed and validated across six diverse datasets ranging from image and audio files to medical scans. The results demonstrate consistent effectiveness in these real-world applications.

Human speech is frequently transmitted through communication channels that introduce distortions, rendering signals susceptible to continuous degradation as transmission progresses. The article introduces a new experimental dataset designed to validate and assess various acoustic similarity checks under such noisy conditions. A novel, hybrid feature set called "HyperOLSA" is proposed; it merges the context-dependent filter bank features from the original OLSA representation with elements of the U50LSA structure. The performance of checks utilizing this HyperOLSA and existing OLSA features was evaluated against the Large Scale Acoustic Similarity Identification (LASI) benchmark. Results indicate that the proposed Hybrid OLSA features do not surpass Original LSA in comparing clean signals or within the specific noise categories present in the dataset. Subsequent analysis of top-10 match outcomes within the dataset identified several recurring acoustic similarities, followed by an examination of non-matching pairs to understand the acoustic boundaries between relevant and irrelevant speech matches.

Data augmentation involves synthesizing new, unlabeled samples from original data to enhance downstream supervised learning tasks. This work investigates data augmentation as a form of data mixing, linking it to successful methods like ensemble learning and the ensemble general bound. Validated by numerical experiments on various tasks and datasets, this approach not only confirms the theory but also provides a straightforward methodology to boost model performance using unsupervised labeled data.

As experimental systems generate increasingly vast amounts of time-tagged data, the need for efficient and flexible data analysis tools becomes increasingly important. The Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA) is a C-based program specifically designed to handle time-tag data effectively, utilizing parallel processing capabilities for a robust performance. By employing vectorized parallel threads during the data accumulation phase and executing thread-safe reduction after the flow concludes—thereby avoiding the pitfalls of trying to synchronize threads during the data accumulation process—ETA achieves superior results. Furthermore, the software incorporates a vital post-accumulation data cleaning step to manage duplicate entries. Testing the program on a 32-core system, where four channels of time-tag data were processed simultaneously, resulted in a throughput of 100 million events per second, a real-world performance of 50 million events per second. What sets the most general version of the data accumulation algorithm apart is its ability to manage different packet sizes, various time tag structures, and different inter-packet intervals. In practical validation, using our facility's two-time-tag system with 400 ps resolution to perform coincidence and correlation measurements on 10^7 events yielded an accurate, noise-free delay distribution.

Furthermore, the corresponding map from characteristics to control strategies is shown to be Lipschitz continuous; this result extends the work of Carmona and co-authors regarding the continuity map from control to characteristic, though our version is more intricate.

User-generated content in the fashion technology field is abundant and includes metrics like generated captions for images, curated online outfit collections, and user-rated fashion products. Driven by the growing popularity of virtual shopping and the significant investment in AI from the fashion industry, we investigate how technological tools can detect inconsistent elements in user-created fashion tasks, specifically matching unrelated items in collections or inappropriate garments in individual items. By analyzing the textual structure of human-generated outfit descriptions, our methods identify linguistic signals that reveal when selected items do not match. We propose two novel algorithms that detect mismatches in both image sets and natural language descriptions. This work includes a comprehensive benchmark using a new, large-scale dataset of over 3.8 million user-created fashion images.

Theories of quantum information under development increasingly rely on general resource models. This paper introduces a specific approach to such models, known as "nonclassical" resources. First rooted in classical resource theories and more recently in the study of coherence (or superpositions), these resources are defined by a set of free operations that preserve classical probability distributions. We examine several aspects of this framework, including necessary and sufficient conditions for a formal definition of free (permutationally invariant) operations, exploring the relationship between different nonclassical resources and establishing a universal link to their underlying quantum analogues. These insights open a new methodological path for constructing and analyzing the spectral resource theories typical in quantum thory. To illustrate its viability, we apply this framework to examine the role of excitation resources in building quantum states within a single qubit system.

Federated learning is a decentralised approach to training machine learning models that ensures privacy by keeping training data local to individual users and only transmitting gradient updates or models to a central server. Although this method offers privacy advantages over traditional learning, its practical deployment is hindered by two main factors: computational constraints on devices and bandwidth limitations for communication. Recent algorithmic attempts to address this dilemma often fail to deliver a balanced combination of privacy and computational efficiency. To mitigate these problems, this paper introduces a new communication and computation algorithm called FedBuff. This algorithm introduces an intermediate aggregation server to reduce direct connections between end devices and the central controller. The server in question uses minimal resources and operates without storing any private data. By routing communications through this infrastructure, FedBuff improves both privacy protection and system scalability. Experimental results demonstrate that it requires less bandwidth and computational power compared to existing methods and can support a significantly larger number of participants.

We outline new theoretical models that enable the formation of primordial black holes (PBCHs) in the mass range of $10^8$ to $10^{11}$ grams following an inflaton decay event. We propose two specific mechanisms—a PBCH-forming channel and a PBCH-nucleating channel—each producing a distinct mass spectrum within this regime. These scenarios are further developed by creating an "all-dark-matter" framework where the inferred existence of dark matter results in an entirely dark matter composed of black hole. In this proposed model, the energy initially stored in the black hole is consumed by absorbing light particles (such as photons and dark photons) through junctions, converting this void-filled state into a stable configuration filled with various forms of radiation and potentially topological defects like strings and membranes that exist until they decay. We calculate the specific power spectra resulting from cosmological expansion and their subsequent redshifting.
