This paper introduces a multi-phase training strategy designed to establish robust canonical poses for 3D objects within the single-view estimation framework. The proposed framework consists of three distinct stages: first, a self-supervised pre-training utilizes simulated objects to learn an initial pose representation; second a back-from-above setup generates further training using estimated poses as ground truths from the first phase to create realistically viewed ground truth; and third, a standard fine-tuning completes the process using standard image-based supervision, where the canonical poses are treated as known. The effectiveness of this approach is validated on the 3DABOW dataset, which contains ground truth for 100 common objects. The new method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, particularly for challenging categories. Additionally, model generalization is tested against objects from the IBO3D dataset, which was designed during the first phase. The results confirm that these methods achieve significantly improved estimation accuracy.

To mitigate these issues, we propose an approach named "Rule-Residual-based Adaptive Generation" (RANG) that accelerates convergence by dynamically modifying network capacity based on model residuals. By monitoring mean and maximal residuals, RANG facilitates timely adjustments of network capacity to align with problem complexity, resulting in significantly quicker optimization and stable convergence. Tested against diverse problems, the RANG method demonstrated superior performance, outperforming comparable strategies by generating more accurate solution operators and values.

While existing library analysis tools have addressed safety issues in specific languages like Java or Python, to our knowledge, none have focused on Rust. This study examines Rust libraries hosted on crates.io to identify and mitigate security risks. By analyzing the top 1 million crates, we find that two-thirds host at least one vulnerability in their latest versions, though installing updates puts the majority of the remaining cases to rest. Additionally, three out of every four libraries depend on at least one "unsafe" sub-crate. Although many of the most critical libraries exhibit high counts of both vulnerabilities and unsafe usage, we discovered a strong tendency for these entities to maintain low update rates. This observation suggests that the presence of "unsafe" code serves as a reliable indicator of potential vulnerabilities, prompting us to introduce and validate the "Safety Index" as a specific metric for assessing Rust library safety. Furthermore, we identify significant patterns in how developers from large corporations fail to update their sub-crates, resulting in prolonged exposure to known vulnerabilities. Finally, we have developed and open-sourced SafetyHub (https://safetyhub.io), a dedicated platform for monitoring Rust library vulnerabilities.

Current dominant representations, which typically map to high-dimensionality vectors of local (often 3D) gradient values, remain highly sensitive to orientation shifts. In many applications, such as cross-domain image retrieval in non-convex settings, this dependence creates challenges that necessitate complex normalization or augmentation procedures. These processes, in turn, degrade both computational efficiency and representation quality. Our study introduces Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) to resolve this issue by converting standard 3D local gradients into low-dimensional asymmetric matrices. We demonstrate that even at ultra-coarse resolution scales, representations derived from 2D LGF matrices exhibit robustness to orientation variance. Empirical results indicate that utilizing LGF-based representations, even augmented with data from multiple orientations, significantly improves both the accuracy and scalability of non-convex image retrieval tasks.

This work addresses enhancing Generalization across Graph Neural Network (GCN) training, a critical yet difficult challenge in applying deep learning to graph data. The core of our novel method, "Scramble GNN," lies in a simple insight: without compromising a GCN's ability to capture local neighborhood information, we can shuffle the order of feature acquisitions during both forward and backward propagation. This modification introduces non-stationarity at every layer of GNNs, effectively randomizing the Graph Convolution operations performed throughout the network. We observe that such non-stationarity mitigates the over-smoothing phenomenon. Empirical results on six standard benchmarks across Semi-Supervised and Transductive Link Prediction tasks confirm that Scramble GNN significantly improves Sibling GNN's performance.

While model inversion attacks have been established as the initial step in real-world model theft, current attacks rely on extracting the full physical model definition, which is inaccessibles. This limitation prevents their use in important scenarios, such as compromising an untrained target with stolen knowledge or functioning against models with unaccessible data. To address these issues, this work introduces Knowledge Extraction, a targeted extraction attack that acquires a proxy model possessing the stolen knowledge of its counterpart without revealing the original model. Since direct model theft is infeasible, this is the first attack of its kind. The attacker guides the learning and training of a target proxy model by acquiring only predictions from the black-box victim. Crucially, all acquired information is confined to simple yes/no outputs, significantly enhancing practicality. The resulting stolen proxy exhibits the same capabilities as the victim and allows a user to access the full internal knowledge and even estimate the victim's inputs by querying the proxy extensively. Knowledge Extraction attacks are more effective and efficient than previous models, enabling the acquisition of robust proxies from state-of-the-art models, successfully executing attacks from single-query to multi-query scenarios, and working effectively under noisy conditions.

Rosie IFU, the surveyor-based instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), is designed to capture spatially resolved maps of extended nebulae and other cosmic structures. It achieves this by creating two-dimensional maps of specific spectral band fluxes and emitting/absolving features across every pixel for target objects. An individual pixel at any location represents a unique line-of-site, each passing through distinct regions of the source with specific widths. Given a model of the target object and observed data points, scientists can infer the source parameters that best explain the observations. In this study, we examine this inverse problem using the Subspace Angular Decomposition (SAD) method. With a configured object model, we test the SAD algorithm's proficiency in retrieving physical parameters—polynomial degrees, source planes, and coefficients—from simulated ROSIE IFU datasets. The SAD approach is particularly well-suited to this endeavor, as it remains efficient in managing high-dimensionality, identifies the underlying structure by reducing it to its core components, and provides robustness against data noise.

We report the identification and characterization of L8S2S-b, the closest (10.8 pc) and most distant (2.5 km/s) neighbor to the Sun among all moving-emission-source brown dwarfs. This discovery relies on high-precision astrometry from the Gaia mission, supplemented with new high-resolution spectroscopy and high-resolution imaging from various ground- and space-based observatories to determine the source's full three-dimensional distance and velocity. Although L8S2S-b appears slightly dimmer in Gaia's main bandpass, it is detected in the satellite's NIRCam, indicating significant excess emission in wider optical windows from an accompanying moving object. This companion likely represents a faint, previously undetected dwarf planet or complex aggregate of small bodies. Consequently, this new system stands as the closest moving-emission-source brown dwarf system and the only one currently known to host a non-pointing extended companion.

This work examines and compares particle production in various particle and nuclear collision scenarios, ranging from deuterons to gold atoms. Focusing on the thermal ratio $K/\pi$, we observe a trend decreasing from high to low energy scales, with values shifting from $\sim 0.15$ in deuteron-deuterium (d-d) collisions down to $\sim 0.05$ in gold-gold (Au-Au) interactions. In contrast, the ratio of yield density to squared slope, $E\frac{1/N}{dN/dt}$, displays the inverse behavior, rising from $0.025$ in d-d collisions to $0.075$ in Au-Au. These opposing trends are explained by different mechanisms: high-energy collisions are dominated by initial parton scattering, whereas the relatively higher $K/\pi$ content in low-energy collisions stems from the mass threshold of kaons. Conversely, the increased $K/\pi$ density in high-energy environments is driven by the higher momentum of kaons. Furthermore, nuclear effects significantly enhance yield density in high-centrality Au-Au collisions, with strangeness showing particularly strong sensitivity to the medium. Nuclear influence is most pronounced in high-energy collisions for p-p cases but is less significant in low-energy contexts.

Furthermore, when galaxy masses are fixed or assumed to follow a galaxy-mass relation based on the data, the calculated SFRs align more closely with the $N$-body values; specifically, the scatter around these SFR estimates decreases significantly with increased use of Br$\gamma$ data. Finally, by comparing Prospector inferences to the stellar mass functions (SMFs) of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field (HUDF) at redshifts of 6 to 9, we observe that the inferred SFR scatter is substantially lower than the scatter in SFRs when assuming a top-down SFR distribution. This paper addresses Team UGS's 2021 UbiComp Challenge solution, aiming to link audio recordings with corresponding handwritten notes for a user performing these actions in an office setting. The workflow involves first extracting time-series sensor data from documents and then using a Vision Transformer to identify specific written characters. Concurrently, a Deep Neural Network analyzes the audio data to extract feature distributions. By comparing these features via cross-correlation, the system pinpoints the timing of each writing stroke. Finally, the proposed approach achieves precise written-to-time mapping with 96.3% accuracy.

This study introduces a novel approach to modeling duration alongside a conventional random forest method. Unlike standard methods that divide duration into discrete histographic bins or assume a single or dual exponential distribution, our technique models the full continuous duration distribution. The core of the approach is the **Meta-Exponential Model**, which characterizes the duration distribution for each class as a mixture of up to two exponential distributions. During training, the forest is divided into leaf nodes, and the number of components in the selected mixture is determined by maximizing a **p-value derived from a hypothesis test**. This test evaluates the null hypothesis, stating that a single-component model is sufficient. If the p-value indicates strong statistical confidence that this null hypothesis is false, the system adopts a two-component (two-exponential) mixture to better describe the data.

The efficacy of the **Meta-Random Forest** was evaluated on the **NSF-PIMACS** dataset, a collection comprising over 10,000 human conversations with manual labels. Accurately identifying where and quantifying how much an organism occupies its habitat is a fundamental ecological research goal. While standard occupancy models handle detection inaccuracies, they often yield a vast number of unidentifiable parameters due to hierarchical structures, necessitating heavy priors that can obscure insights. This study introduces a Bayesian framework utilizing a novel multivariate prior to significantly simplify vector parameter estimation in occupancy modeling, thereby easing interpretation. After explaining the method and its application to vector parameter constraints, we examine the impact of misspecified multivariate priors on estimation. Finally, we analyze how detection probabilities vary under different scenarios to test the prior's behavior. The proposed approach is significantly more efficient for vector parameter identification and interpretation.

This paper presents an analysis of the SKincare project, which introduces a SKincare diagnostic system for patients that enables general practitioners to identify and refer those requiring specialist attention. Recent research has shown that approximately 70% of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) exhibit an excess in ultraviolet and blue light during the early phases of their explosions. To address this discrepancy, we developed the `fc` model, which incorporates an additional correlation term representing the perturbation of variability driven by specific physical deviations. Applying the `fc` model to a dataset of 70 multi-wavelength observations from 56 specific SNe Ia, we found that it successfully reproduces the majority of data points and extends predictive capabilities into the early post-explosion period, where previous models were less effective. Although a small residual uncertainty remains, we argue that this stems from observational limits rather than a deficiency in the model's core mechanics. Ultimately, the enhanced `fc` model offers additional value as a pre-explosion screen; it can identify data-point incompatibilities that may result from reporting errors or signify unusual host-system events, provided further improvements are pursued.

A new laboratory study investigates steady-state particle-entrained plumes by applying an analytical framework that expresses entrainment as the sum of three distinct components: those driven by density stratification above and below the plume interface caused by the source buoyancy flux $\beta$, and those induced by the effective mean particle settling velocity $\alpha$. Entraination rates $\nu$ were measured using a laser-based imaging system for plumes with negative and positive particle buoyancy flux $\alpha$. The results indicate that $\beta$-induced entrainment is symmetric, while velocity-induced and interaction terms cause a net increase in the effective particle settling velocity. Notably, when the plume buoyancy flux $\beta$ opposes the particle buoyancy flux, a net resuspension of particles can occur, causing their mean velocity to point upward.

This study introduces a novel stochastic infection model based on a configuration model for contagion within hypergraphs, alongside a corresponding coalescent process defined on infected subgraphs. The contagion dynamics are influenced by three specific factors: the frequency of contact involving multiple individuals, the count of people within each contact group, and the size of such groups themselves. We derive a differential equation that accurately approximates the evolution of the susceptible population during the infectious phase, with our findings corroborated by extensive agent-based simulations. Furthermore, a key contribution is a universal coalescent model capable of reconstructing the initial emergence and widespread adoption of an infection. In a specific application of these methods, the researchers analyzed the collective behaviors on a well-known online platform, successfully identifying the origin of two distinct "cultural waves."

We introduce a discrete-generation population model incorporating geographic dispersion, where individuals occupy an infinite one-dimensional lattice, each holding a single active gene with arbitrary but fixed ancestry at a specific locus. At every step, a distinct individual emerges at a uniform probability among all lattice sites, with its parent selected according to the Wright-Fisher framework. Simultaneously, we integrate a Poissonian migration mechanism, allowing adjacent lattice neighbors to exchange positions at a constant probability. At the critical parameter value where migration ceases to affect the limiting population structure, our analysis reveals that the system's behavior is indistinguishable from the standard coalescent with point mutations. Furthermore, we detail a continuous range of migration probabilities extending beyond this critical threshold that likewise leave the limit law unchanged. When migration operates above the critical rate, the population's limit structure mirrors that of the Cannings model featuring proportional variance var(π(i))∼σ^(2)s_(i)×(n−s\_(i))/ (n^2), where the allele frequency profile π*(i) sums to the proportion of individuals in allele (i), with n representing the population size, thereby capturing the underlying structure of the population's genetic composition at the specific genetic locus under study.

Artificial attention mechanisms have been widely integrated across various subdomains of speech processing. This study examines the impact of adding attention layers to existing artificial neural networks for the detection of spoofing artifacts. Our available corpus includes a training set with 200,000 samples and a hold-out testing set with 50,000 samples, both drawn from a single physical speaker. Our findings reveal that incorporating attention enhances performance, yielding a 3% relative improvement in detection rate and a 30% relative reduction in computational cost. Beyond these quantitative gains, our results suggest that attention provides specific benefits in analyzing spoofing attacks, a perspective we explore and elaborate upon.

We investigate the relationships linking supergravity, various formulations of quantum gravity, and both high- and low-energy effective theories, specifically examining their interplay in the context of branes and gravity propagating in anti-de de Sitter (AdS) spaces. We introduce and investigate a directional nonlinearity in a silicon microdisk, where an optical c-wave directionally excites localized surface acoustic waves. This mechanism enables unique findings: first, comparing generated pairs of correlated photon pairs reveals that their coherence functions invert when the pump beam's propagation is reversed; second, this inversion occurs solely when the acoustic beam path remains fixed. These observations provide direct evidence of directional nonlinearities and define a mechanism for controlling photon-pair coherence via acoustic wave direction. Consequently, we establish a foundation for developing optoacoustic schemes that can independently regulate the quantum characteristics of light using acoustic waveguides.

Cuprous oxide etching of silicon offers a technique yielding insulators with significantly lower surface defect densities than conventional methods. However, available thin etched silicon (PE-Si) samples exhibit a high resistance that is orders of magnitude less than expected based on bulk material properties. To investigate this discrepancy, we measured temperature and magnetic field dependencies of resistance and the Hall effect. Analysis of these measurements indicates the PE-Si resistance and Hall effect are consistent with bulk unetched silicon, suggesting the observed properties are intrinsic to the silicon and not extrinsic. In contrast, we found that the carrier concentration in these etched silicons is approximately one order of magnitude lower than that in buffer-oxide-etched silicon.

Existing literature suggests that Commodity Trading Advisors (CTAs) function as contrarian traders who benefit from the short-term reversal effect. This paper investigates the relationship between CTAs and the demand for website visits. The findings reveal a positive and robust correlation between specific CTA activities and website traffic, a pattern that persists across various robustness checks. Additionally, we explore the mechanisms underlying this link, observing that the evidence remains strong among routes that facilitate rapid and anonymous access. Finally, we address potential alternative explanations for these findings, proposing that algorithmic systems might inadvertently capitalize on short-term reversal effects simply by monitoring CTA trading behavior.

Systematic extrapolation involves applying a model trained to generate and evaluate counts up to a specific threshold $N_{cap}$ as a counting system for reaching significantly larger scales. Recent research has demonstrated that modern neural architectures possess the capacity for super-generalization, allowing them to handle counts far beyond their initial training limits ($N_{cap}$) using a technique known as systematic extrapolation. However, a critical unresolved question remains: can these neural models also extrapolate this counting capability to arbitrarily large scales? This study investigates the limits of neural system generalization by employing super-generalization to count up to extremely large numbers (approximately $10^5$) within standard deep visual generalization benchmarks where counts previously appeared arbitrary. By utilizing non-Markovian dynamics and data from regimes with both small and large $N_{cap}$ values, the findings indicate that systematic extrapolation in this regime does not exhibit signs of super-generalization, remaining confined within the original training capacity ($N_{cap}$) rather than extending far beyond it. Furthermore, the results demonstrate an inverse relationship between $N_{cap}$ and the maximum count achieved via extrapolation, suggesting there is no point at which counting capacity explodes. We observe that all tested neural architectures, including CTRN, CFRNNs, and LSTMs, behave similarly in this regard, remaining limited to their trained capacities, and suggest this limitation may be an inherent characteristic of the deep recurrent architectures themselves.

In supervised machine learning, humans manually annotate training data; however, full labeling of every dataset is often unaffordable. A more viable strategy involves "selective labeling," where a subset of data is carefully acquiried to optimize performance. This process, or data selection, faces the challenge that the value of individual data points remains hard to evaluate without a pre-existing model, as their utility is intertwined with the model itself. Previous methods typically analyze feature data through univariate or pairwise lenses, often overlooking the most valuable instances. In this work, we establish that a "maximizing acquired information" (MAFI) approach provides the optimal solution for data selection. We prove a gap bound showing that the gap between the MAFI Method's performance and any suboptimal strategy depends on the total number of available labels; this gap increases exponentially with data amount, meaning even modest label constraints can result in significantly lower optimization outcomes. Furthermore, we introduce a practical algorithm, D³, based on this principle, which is supported by efficient approximation strategies to calculate the optimal selection. Our D³ system achieves near-optimal results, and extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods.

This work defines and investigates "the prime gap polynomial," a concept essential for understanding twin primes and identifying their generators. We demonstrate that a given pair of primes constitutes twin primes if and only if their (unique) prime gap polynomial is prime. We also analyze how these polynomials are linked to quadratic fields, sieve methods, and sieved sets. In so doing, we develop a specific sieve capable of generating all twin primes. Furthermore, this tool isolates the generators of twin prime candidates, establishing a sequence of integer pairs where each element is the prime gap polynomial for some twin prime.

This study introduces a multi-tier control strategy that empowers autonomous-level mobile robots with sonar equipment to detect and circumvent obstacles. The system consists of three layers: the lowest layer utilizes a Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithm based on a Taped-Switched (TTS) graph to manage local obstacle avoidance and path planning; the middle layer implements a Global Map Builder that constructs the environment and determines the optimal trajectory for the sensor to follow. The highest layer simulates physical laws and deduces obstacle properties from sonar data. In experimental trials, this hierarchical approach demonstrated effective obstacle navigation, successful priority handling for predefined paths, the capability to infer object dimensions from sonar readings, and the potential to estimate soft-matter characteristics.

By anticipating future requirements and performing multiple prediction rounds for accuracy, the framework enhances the efficiency of that predictability. Experimental validation across diverse benchmarks confirms dynamically SOAR outperforms CUDA by an average margin of 1.55×. It surpasses two prominent advanced GPU memory projects, SOAR and SPD, achieving performance gains of 1.41× and 1.42×, respectively.

Impurity-induced phonon phonon interactions in superfluids can trigger a phase transition to a supersolid state characterized by a minimum in its roton energy. This study examines how a roton-minimum-forming mass behaves when moved periodically within a one-dimensional supersolid. It is established that the associated impurity motion couples with the host supersolid's phonons. Notably, driving the defect via high-frequency oscillations at intensities sufficient to classically average out the potential energy effectively smooths the supersolid's structure. Furthermore, the study confirms that before the phase transition to a supersolid occurs, one can entangle the ideal Bose gas with the oscillating defect. By tuning system parameters, it is possible to modulate both the formation of the supersolid and the parameters governing this entangled state. Consequently, this mechanism offers a novel pathway for generating and manipulating supersolid states as well as producing supersolid-sensor based quantum states.

Our simulations reveal that the density field exhibits anisotropy, with clustering along radial and tangential directions becoming more pronounced at larger scales. Additionally, we examined how initial conditions, galaxy mass, and the strength of gas cooling and radiation influences influence the density field's structural properties. Although a clear, consistent large-scale anisotropic pattern in galaxy-scale molecular structures is difficult to establish without injecting these external factors, our findings suggest that once such influences from stars and radiation are accounted for, anisotropic structures in a galactic nuclear region like the CMZ could emerge early in its evolution.

We present the "quantum scissors," a method for preparing multipartite entangled beams of polarized photons, which is a fundamental step in the construction of quantum networks and quantum computers utilizing the polarization degree of freedom. For the $N=2$ case, involving a two-photon entangled state of polarization, this approach employs a simple beam splitter to entangle a single-photon superposition. Subsequently, we generalize the "quantum scissors" framework to enable the preparation of two-photon or $N$-photon entangled states of any arbitrary order ($\ge 2$). Using a two-port device where only input port 1 receives a two-photon or $N$-photon entangled state, we obtain at the device's ports a output beam of polarized photons for that same dimension $N$. Notably, we find that for $N \ge 3$, simply tracing out (discarding) the photons at port 2 from the full joint state yields exactly the desired $N$-photon entangled state of polarization at the ports. This outcome holds regardless of the specific reduced density matrix character or the degree of polarization mode mismatch between the input beam and the device itself.

Over the past few years, Internet of Things (IoT) technology has rapidly expanded across every facet of human life, rapidly increasing both the number of IoT devices and the diverse types available. Despite this growth, there has been little investigation into classifying these devices in an economically efficient manner. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a novel, supervised, cost-aware framework for IoT device classification that minimizes overall classification expenses. This method considers three specific costs: the direct classification cost for each device type, the misclassification risk per type, and the opportunity cost of delayed detection for each type. By integrating a Bayesian decision rule, the approach calculates the optimal decision rule to achieve the lowest possible total misclassification and delay risks. Furthermore, it implements an efficient kv-stream algorithm that enables near real-time device classification with minimal computational cost. By incorporating a mechanism to weigh the misclassification risk specific to each device type, it extends traditional classification methods to include a quantitative assessment of risk. The algorithm's efficacy has been empirically verified through simulations using both synthetic data and real-world datasets, demonstrating that while per-class processing time may be longer, it successfully delivers a significant reduction in the total risk.

Liquid foams function as a multiphase material where a continuous liquid phase supports a network of gas. Surface tension within the interfaces drives the liquid from the bulk into the solidly packed plate structures, impeding flow and inducing a yield stress; this stress diminishes as the material's surface becomes smoother. Our research establishes a method for characterizing the microstructural yield stress, exploring its relationship with roughness, and analyzing the deformation of yield stress foams through a yield stress model. By applying a discrete element framework, we simulated rough yield stress foams, utilizing the Janssen method to compute their yield stress in various configurations. Our findings demonstrate a predictable decrease in yield stress as a roughness parameter is reduced, with the model's accuracy for yield stress reaching high precision (a coefficient of determination R² = 0.961). Furthermore, we developed a simplified, one-dimensional microstructural model that closely replicates these results. By integrating our computational simulations with the proposed simplified framework, we have created a dual approach for characterizing the mechanical properties of yield stress foams. Ultimately, this study offers insights into the yield behavior of complex, yield stress-forming foams by analyzing specific variables such as the size of bubbles and the mechanical properties of the gas-liquid interface.

This study investigates the statistical distributions of active forces required to sustain a particle at a fixed position within an anharmonic potential, a problem with relevance to biological contexts. These findings carry significant weight for characterizing force distributions in natural systems.

We introduce a proposed method for generating petawatt-scale, soft X-ray free-electron laser (XFELO) seeding using a high-current electron box current, complemented by a dedicated low-energy undulator section, with a beam current of approximately 5A. This method is based on a dual-stage configuration: the first stage produces a strong XFELO seeding output, while the second involves tapering the electron current in an undulator to amplify this seed. This second-stage linear energy extraction yields exceptionally high photon intensity, as the output power is directly proportional to the available stored XFELO power. Our calculations suggest that combining XFELO seeding with undulator depletion can achieve pulse intensities of roughly $10^{17}\, \mathrm{W/cm^2}$. Such output represents a significant advancement, potentially enabling the investigation of previously inaccessible physical phenomena and offering superior capabilities across scientific domains including atomic and molecular science, optics, and imaging.

Predicting events in dynamic graphs is crucial for applications like understanding drug interactions, tracking how ideas evolve within academic fields, and modeling the spread of misinformation. Most methods model this as linking two nodes with a specific event type, but they struggle to capture the full context because the graph's structure changes as new data arrives. Existing techniques often rely on embedding node pairs directly into an event representation or using static graph embeddings; both approaches fail to account for the graph's temporal dynamics. This paper introduces DyGED (Dynamic Graph Embedding for Event Detection), a framework that utilizes the local graph embedding of nodes in a node-type-dependent manner. Unlike other models, this flexible approach allows for simultaneous training on both known and unseen event types. Specifically, it estimates a latent embedding for each unknown type by comparing it against the embeddings of the involved nodes and the current local graph structure. During testing on test data containing unknown events, the model projects these new instances into the existing type-space to find the most compatible event category based on the closest pre-trained embedding. Evaluation across multiple datasets reveals that this dynamic projection mechanism outperforms strong baselines, marking it as the top-performing method in all scenarios.

The paper introduces an approach to creating Guderley problem solutions for any power-law equation of state via analytical means. We explicitly compute corresponding hydrodynamic and energetic quantities in the self-similar limit. These calculations are specifically intended to benchmark numerical simulations against non-periodic, Guderley-type shock problems and to validate the results using hydrodynamic codes via convergence tests in the self-similar regime. Transparency remains a critical objective in Explainable AI (XAI), a domain where Requirements Engineering (RE) practices can significantly enhance transparency through the management of system specifications. While XRE (Extreme RE) has been applied to critical systems, these applications often lack comprehensive insights into how RE activities function within non-reliability contexts. Consequently, XRE's utility for explaining AI systems—frequently perceived as non-critical—remains both underexplored and underutilized. This paper investigates the intersection of RE and AI specifically through two lenses: (1) how RE activities can be adapted to AI development contexts, and (2) how XRE functions as a mechanism for explaining artificial intelligence.

Adenomas in the colon and rectum are precursors to the most common form of cancer in this area. Conventional morphological classifications and numerical assessments of adenomous structures aim to predict patient risk levels and determine necessary surveillance intervals or treatments for managing precancerous or early-stage cancers. This research introduces a methodology utilizing deep neural networks for the classification and grading of adenomous tissue through a dataset of 34,000 microscopic images. We compared two distinct approaches: an image-centric model and a histology-agnostic one. The image-centric approach employed state-of-the-art Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures for multi-class and multi-label image classification, achieving a test-set Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.80 and F1 score of 0.70. Conversely, the tissue-agnostic strategy involved training a deep feed-forward neural network to predict morphological attributes from low-dimensional image embeddings; this method yielded a significantly higher AUC of 0.87 and an F1 score of 0.80. We also assessed the potential cause of over-fitting in the image-centric system and examined the transferability of these techniques to other tissue types beyond adnomas.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) faces challenges with the highly nonconvex, high-dimensional landscape of its variational parameters, particularly in large-scale quantum computing contexts. While quantum computing theoretically offers an advantage in handling such complexity, current methods are often inefficient. Addressing this, we introduce a strategy to tackle high-dimensional variational problems by utilizing Bayesian optimization (BO) alongside a quantum-based kernel for QAOA. Our analysis demonstrates that this BO approach requires fewer function evaluations than standard, naive optimization methods, thereby improving the efficiency of both QAOA and BO specifically for large dimensions. Furthermore, we propose a BO initialization technique that leverages the specific structural features of the quantum kernel's kernel trick. This initialization significantly accelerates convergence by narrowing the initial parameter search space. To experimentally validate this framework, a simulated QAOA for the Boolean Satisfiability problem DSAT was implemented; our results confirm that this BO optimization strategy outperforms the standard optimization, providing the QAOA circuit with a superior initial parameter guess.

Reinforcement learning offers a computational approach to addressing the derivation of the Gibbs measure, a technique especially effective in handling high-dimensional systems. This study focuses on bandit settings and demonstrates how various actor-critic algorithms determine the Gaussian approximation associated with this measure. In the process, we also propose an algorithm capable of computing the invariant distribution for Markov decision processes.

Although Hubbard model quantum fluctuations favor a homogeneous Fermi liquid, they can stabilize ordered phases when coupled with long-range repulsive interactions. In Hubbard systems exhibiting stripe order, we demonstrate that this structure persists and shows significant resilience even against a broad spectrum of homogeneous exchange and long-range attractive interactions, including Hubbard terms combined with $1/r$ or $1/r^2$ forces. Our analytical framework assumes a static background that dynamically reacts through dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), a method validated by supportive numerical simulations. This contrast between our result and existing theoretical perspectives suggests that long-range interactions can drive stable competitive ordered states, a finding with direct implications for strongly correlated electron systems.

Identifying the centroid of a vertebra is essential for spine segmentation and other clinical applications. Current automated methods typically rely on deep learning or regional testing, but they often struggle with accuracy. This research introduces a novel center identification technique that augments the traditional region convolution process with a specialized convolution designed to enhance feature representation. By leveraging both global and localized features, this new approach creates a comprehensive feature mapping that allows for more precise calculation of the center within the region. Experiments conducted on two public datasets demonstrate that this method improves identification accuracy by at least 5% compared to three current state-of-the-art techniques.

We map the algebro-structural makeup of Markovian models onto features of their dynamics to create streamlined formulas for asymptotic convergence rates, averaging processes, and integrals of correlation functions. Applying this method within a framework of multi-scale quantum dynamics, where both the initial state and Hamiltonian carry arbitrary frequency components, yields a unified expression for any correlation integral. This approach explicitly sets up such integrals as a sum of terms involving specific model parameters, where each term pairs a subset of decay modes with corresponding correlation terms from the input model, alongside an integral over a single stationary correlation function. Consequently, our technique merges different computational methods into one, offering a standardized process to implement and choose between them.

Furthermore, we examine how inaccuracies change with increasing frequency. The findings reveal that this deviation is heavily dependent on specific material properties, generally becoming negligible to zero at extremely high frequencies.

We introduce a spatially adaptive photonic setup designed to probe nonlinearities within polariton condensons. This approach offers a robust strategy for identifying and analyzing novel two-dimensional semiconductor materials through non-invasive means.

This essay argues that we can identify specific instances in the extant records where Galileo felt free from the strict bounds of empiricism, notably when he analyzed the language and evidence foundational to his work. Focusing on his discussions of "weight," or *pescio*—a term encompassing various related concepts—this article proposes that Galiano's observations on the linguistic and semantic underpinnings of "weight" reveal a deeper understanding and more critical reflection on the scientific principles underpinning his own findings.

To investigate key macroscopic magnetic events—such as island coalescence, which drives the rapid ($\sim$ millisecond) hard X-ray flares observed during solar eruptions—a newly developed 1.5D model has been applied. This algorithm for magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) evolution couples the large-scale flow with specialized solvers for a diverse set of reconnection algorithms, including standard outflow-reconnection, multi-point (multi-X) mechanisms, and hybrid approaches, all adhering to selected reconnection rates. By executing simulations across varying guide magnetic fields and initial tearmode amplitudes, the study evaluates the causes and consequences associated with different reconnection mechanisms. Results demonstrate that for fast coalescence, the chosen reconnection rate largely dictates the specific mechanism: both hybrid models and fixed-rate mechanisms can reproduce observational data, yet the underlying reconnection processes in these two cases can be entirely distinct. Although MHD governs the broad-scale island dynamics, the ultimate interaction points and speed are determined at the kinetic scale, where reconnection physics operates. The findings suggest that a single, universal solar universal reconnection rate is unlikely; rather, the appropriate rate may co-vary with the specific plasma mechanisms driving reconnection.

How do digital helpers form reasonable plans across extended interactions involving uncertainty, and how do they acquire cognitive strategies and intuitive insights as experts through on-going human collaboration? This study investigates these problems in the context of cooperative Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (cpomdp). Specifically, a specific class of problems is examined where the optimal policy for the agent can be expressed in terms of "basic strategies," defined as sequences of actions and information states. These fundamental approaches are shown to allow the other team members to cultivate intuitive cognitive models of their partner's behavior. By analyzing these strategies over time, the analysis demonstrates that the builder can develop improved approximations of the most effective simple strategies, thereby enabling the agent to execute plans that display increasingly sophisticated capabilities. Consequently, the team can expand the range of joint tasks they can execute.
